issues.legal_issue: A sub-lessee whose possession results from a subletting prohibited by law and who is treated as a trespasser is excluded from statutory protection for ryotwari sub-lessees.
material_facts: A recorded tenant granted a five-year sublease despite a statutory prohibition on subletting that applied to him.
The governing law treated a person who obtained possession through a prohibited sublease as a trespasser.
The sub-lessees sought to rely on a protection enactment that excluded sub-lessees treated as trespassers.
issues.conclusion: The sub-lessees were not entitled to protection under the ryotwari sub-lessee protection enactment.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 73 and 78 of the Revenue Administration and Ryotwari Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950 prohibited the subletting at issue and treated a person obtaining possession through a contravening sublease as a trespasser. Section 3 of the Madhya Bharat Ryotwari Sub-lessee Protection Act, 1955 excluded such a trespasser from its protection; the Act's definition of a ryotwari sub-lessee did not include a person whose prohibited lease was void. The contrary observation in Rao Nihalkaran v. Ramchandra, [1963] M.P.L.J. 314, was disapproved as inconsistent with the express statutory text.

predicates.claim_seeks_sublessee_protection: The person in possession sought statutory protection for possession obtained as a sub-lessee.
predicates.sublease_violated_rental_restriction: The tenant granted a sublease in circumstances in which the governing law prohibited subletting.
predicates.sublessee_was_legally_treated_as_trespas: The governing law treated the person who obtained possession through the prohibited sublease as a trespasser.
predicates.governing_law_excluded_trespassers_from_: The protection scheme excluded sub-lessees whom the governing law treated as trespassers.

issues.definition: When a person seeks protection as a sub-lessee, the sublease violated a rental restriction, the person was treated as a trespasser, and the protection scheme excluded trespassers, protection is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A person excluded from the statutory class of protected ryotwari sub-lessees does not acquire occupancy-tenant status under the successor land-revenue code on the basis of that sublease.
material_facts: The sublease was prohibited, and the sub-lessees were treated as trespassers under the governing law.
The protection enactment excluded the sub-lessees from protection, so they did not qualify as ryotwari sub-lessees under its definition.
The High Court held that the sub-lessees acquired occupancy-tenant rights under the successor land-revenue code; the appeal challenged that holding.
issues.conclusion: The sub-lessees did not acquire occupancy-tenant status under the successor land-revenue code, and the High Court's order was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 185(1)(ii)(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959 conferred occupancy-tenant status on a person holding land as a ryotwari sub-lessee as defined by the Madhya Bharat Ryotwari Sub-lessee Protection Act, 1955. Because a person whose prohibited lease was void and who was excluded from that Act's protection did not fall within that defined class, the person could not obtain occupancy-tenant status under section 185(1)(ii)(b). The contrary observation in Rao Nihalkaran v. Ramchandra, [1963] M.P.L.J. 314, was disapproved as contrary to the express statutory provisions.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges occupancy status claimed through a sublease that violated a rental restriction, the person was treated as a trespasser and fell outside the defined protected sub-lessee class, occupancy-tenant status is not acquired.
